item.title: Arrests after far-right protesters attack police in The Hague
item.description:
Arrests after far-right protesters attack police in The Hague

September 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Police have made 24 arrests in The Hague after an anti-immigration march in The Hague organised by a far-right group turned violent.

Several hundred people gathered at the site near Centraal Station at around 11am after a group calling itself Wij Zijn Het Volk (“We are the people”) announced the event, exactly a year after a similar demonstration descended into a full-blown riot.

Protesters wearing balaclavas, scarves and masks to cover their faces gave Nazi salutes and carried banners with racist slogans such as “remigratie” (remig “blanke mannen vooraan” (“white men first”).

Acting mayor Richard de Mos ordered riot police to clear the Malieveld after demonstrators attacked police and ignored earlier orders to remove face coverings.

The rioters threw smoke bombs and fireworks and ripped traffic poles out of the ground, at least one of which was hurled at police. Police beat back the crowd towards Centraal Station using dogs, pepper spray and batons, managing to restore order by 3.30pm.

However, the violence was less extreme than a year ago, when 1,000 rioters set fire to police cars, blockaded the A12 motorway and smashed windows at the offices of political party D66.

“Atrocious”

Justice minister David van Weel called the scenes “atrocious” in a post on social media site X, while De Mos said the violence directed at police “crossed a line”.

“Hitler salutes, anti-Semitic chants, violence against police and fireworks thrown at riot squad officers,” Van Weel said. “It’s important that these people are dealt with severely.”

“That is why we cancelled the march and only allowed a demonstration on the Malieveld,” De Mos said. “When the violence continued, it was necessary to put an end to it.”

Walgelijke beelden vanaf het Malieveld. Hitlergroeten, antisemitische leuzen, geweld tegen de politie en vuurwerk gooien naar de ME. Belangrijk dat hier snoeihard tegen opgetreden wordt. Dank aan alle agenten die weer voor onze rechtsstaat staan.https://t.co/31JadLNBjJ

— David van Weel (@ministerjenv) September 19, 2026

item.title: Dutch destinations: Check out the highs and lows of Maastricht
item.description:
Dutch destinations: Check out the highs and lows of Maastricht

September 19, 2026 Molly Quell

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

One of the oldest cities in the Netherlands, Maastricht lies in the southern part of the country, close to both the Belgian and German borders. It is no wonder that the founding treaty of the European Union was signed there, nor that the Belgian (and French) influence has created a food mecca.

No one can quite agree on its exact origins. Celts lived in the area at least as far back as the 5th century BC, and the Romans showed up about 600 years later to build a bridge over the Meuse River that now runs through the centre of the city. Maastricht played a vital role in the Carolingian Empire and the Holy Roman Empire, and its location made it quite coveted between the 16th and 18th centuries. Many of those fortifications are still standing.

It was the first Dutch city to be liberated by the Allies during World War II. Half-century later, the city hosted a series of councils that led to the signing of the Maastricht Treaty, which paved the way toward the establishment of the European Union and the euro.

Maastricht is now home for 125,000 people, including many of the students studying at nearby Maastricht University.

Five things to do

Enjoy the city’s long and storied past with a historic walk.

Start at the Vrijthof, the main square where Dutch conductor André Rieu holds his summer concert series and which turns into a Christmas market in the winter.

Vrijthof is home to the majestic Basilica of Saint Servatius, where Maastricht’s patron saint Servatius is said to have died in 384 AD. A stone church was built over his grave in the 6th century which has been gradually expanded to the looming structure you see today.

You can loop past Our Lady, Star of the Sea (Sterre der Zee), a popular pilgrimage site, and see the famous wooden statue of Mary that dates to the 15th century.

Walk under the Helpoort (Hell’s Gate), the oldest city gate in the whole of the Netherlands, and then stroll through the Stadspark. On a nice day, you can join the many students who spread out a blanket and enjoy a few beers in the sun.

The part is also home to a number of sculptures and art installations. You can walk along the city walls and even see a statue of the fourth musketeer d’Artagnan. The leader of King Louis XIV’s elite corps of gentlemen, died in battle in 1673 during the French siege of Maastricht and archaeologists recently announced they may have discovered his skeletal remains under the floorboards of a nearby church.

If you want to go deeper into history, go underground
You can tour the caves of Mount Saint Peter, a collection of limestone quarries which date back to the 13th century. During World War II, they were used to safeguard arms and valuables from the Germans, including The Night Watch by Rembrandt van Rijn which was removed from its frame and rolled into a cylinder.

You can also walk through the casemates (kazematten), defensive corridors that run under the city. These structures are unique in the Netherlands, as the groundwater level is too high in other parts of the country.

Visit a bookstore
The 700-year-old Dominicanenkerk has quite the history. Along with serving as a house of worship, the church has been used as a warehouse, an archive, a printing house, and even a place to store bikes. Napoleon used it to store equipment and military personnel while invading the region in the 1790s.

It was converted into one of Europe’s most unique bookstores following a restoration project in the mid 2000s. If that’s not enough, you can also check out De Tribune, which was named the best literary bookstore in the Netherlands in 2024.

Shop til you drop
Maastricht is known for its shopping and the city is filled with boutiques, art galleries, vintage shops and more. The Rechtstraat is just one of many lovely shopping streets. On Wednesday and Fridays, the city holds a market with Friday wares more orientated towards clothing. On Saturday, hundreds of vendors turn out for the antiques market.

Go to the other extreme
Just outside Maastricht, you can find the highest point in the Netherlands. At a little over 322 metres tall, the Vaalserberg might merely be considered an average hill in other countries, but for the Netherlands, that’s a mountain.

It’s also home to Drielandenpunt, a three country-point where the borders of Belgium, Germany, and the Netherlands meet. Its lookout towers offer great views of the surrounding region.

Where to eat

Limburgse vlaai is the local delicacy and a must have on any trip to Maastricht. It’s not quite a pie and it’s not quite a pastry, but it’s definitely delicious. De Bisschopsmolen currently has no less than nine on the menu at their bakery and cafe. If you’d like to try your hand at making your own, they also host vlaai workshops.

The Onze Lieve Vrouweplein has a collection of outdoor cafes where you can enjoy a coffee or a beer.

If you want a fancy meal, look to L’Auberge. This lovely restaurant sits in the former stables of Château Neercanne. For an even fancier meal, the companion Restaurant Château Neercanne. For a real treat, you can stay at the hotel.

Cycle outside of the city and have lunch at Grand-Café Buitengoed Slavante. The country estate has a great breakfast menu and you can also take a walk on the grounds.

Another great lunch option in the city is the hip, Marres Kitchen. It’s in the same building as the museum Marres, House for Contemporary Culture so enjoy some art at the same time.

Where to stay

For a boutique experience, try Townhouse Hotel Maastricht. It also offers apartments if you’d like to eat your vlaai at home. Kruisherenhotel is the only five star hotel in the region. It’s housed in a 15th century monastery along the Kommelplein and each one of its 60 guest rooms features unique art and decor. The the Easy Hotel is a clean and cheap choice.

How to get there

The train stops practically in the middle of the city and you can walk in along a beautifully landscaped boulevard. It’s about three hours from Amsterdam. The drive is a bit shorter, at 2.5 hours, depending on the traffic.

Anything else

Keep in mind that Maastricht is south of the river and therefore deep into Carnival territory. Andre Rieu’s summer concerts are extremely popular and thus make it impossible to find hotels and parking.

item.title: Man targeted in village shooting arrested over cocaine shipment
item.description:
Man targeted in village shooting arrested over cocaine shipment

September 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The man whose farmhouse was besieged by dozens of gunmen in a suspected drugs feud has been arrested in Germany, Dutch media report.

German police said a 28-year-old man was detained in a car park in Soest, 150km beyond the Dutch border in North Rhine-Westphalia, on suspicion of trying to smuggle nearly four tonnes of cocaine through the French port of Dunkirk.

NOS quoted sources saying the suspect was Jan G., who is believed to have been the target of a group of heavily armed men who killed a security guard and injured two police officers in a shoot-out in Overasselt, Gelderland, three weeks ago.

Police traced G. in the wake of the shooting, as well as another man who was arrested in Dordrecht a week ago in connection with the drugs shipment.

French customs officers said the cocaine, with an estimated value of €225 mln, was concealed among plastic waste in a container from Ghana.

The Telegraaf reported that the shipment belonged to Jos Leijdekkers, known as “Bolle Jos”, the Dutch drugs baron at the top of Europol’s list of most wanted fugitives. The cross-border police force has issued a €200,000 reward for information leading to his capture.

G.’s house was closed on the orders of local mayor Joerie Minses, who also ordered the man to stay out of the village for three months in an attempt to restore order.

Some 33 men of varying nationalities, including Dutch, French, Algerian and Belgian, were arrested in the wake of the shooting on September 1. Six were from the Amsterdam area. Some were caught while hiding in fields or trying to flee the area by car or train.

Judges ordered all but one of the suspects to be detained in custody for the next three months while investigations continue.

item.title: Indian restaurant owners arrested in human trafficking inquiry
item.description:
Indian restaurant owners arrested in human trafficking inquiry

September 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Two owners of a chain of Indian restaurants in the Netherlands have been arrested as part of an investigation into suspected human trafficking.

Europol and the Dutch labour inspectorate carried out a probe into allegations that a rule making it easier for Asian restaurants to hire specialist chefs from outside the EU was being widely abused.

The restaurant owners are said to have hired staff from India as chefs but employed them in non-specialist roles such as cleaning, washing up or waiting tables.

Labour inspectors also found the employees were working between 60 and 80 hours a week, rather than the 38 that was allowed under the terms of their work permit, and were being underpaid or not paid at all for the extra hours.

The two suspects owned eight restaurants that were part of a nationwide chain with branches in Utrecht, Amsterdam, The Hague, Hilversum and Hoofddorp.

Europol said around 70 staff had been hired on false premises, contributing around €4 million of unpaid labour. The investigation also covered allegations of similar abuses in Belgium, Germany, Luxembourg and Switzerland.

The owners arranged their workers’ housing and allegedly fined them if they left before the end of their contract, which deterred the victims from contacting authorities.

“There are also indications that their families in their home countries were put under pressure and threatened with violence by the suspects in order to make the victims work harder and prevent them complaining to the managers of the restaurant chain,” the inspectors wrote.

The Dutch government introduced a simplified work permit system for Asian chefs in 2019 to address a labour shortage, but scrapped it three years later after inspectors found evidence that it was being abused by employers.

Inspectors visited 50 restaurants in 2021 and 2022 in a mix of randomised checks and others targeting high-risk establishments, which found 60% of the high-risk restaurants and 45% that were selected at random breached the rules at least once.

item.title: Muslims launch hotline to report attacks on Dutch mosques
item.description:
Muslims launch hotline to report attacks on Dutch mosques

September 18, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Muslim liaison organisation CMO has set up a national hotline to report attacks on Dutch mosques amid concern that many incidents are going unreported.

Police have admitted that discrimination is underreported in the Netherlands, while community leaders hope the hotline will encourage victims to come forward.

Muhsin Köktas, chair of the CMO, said he believed the online portal, which will go live on September 20, “will lower the threshold for our community to report incidents here”.

Last year 414 cases of discrimination against Muslims were reported to police, 20 of which came from mosques, but Köktas said many crimes were not reported “because often nothing happens or if someone reports an incident, they don’t know what happens with it afterwards”.

A police spokesman said the force was aware of the low reporting rate, but urged victims to come forward.

“In broad terms discrimination is rarely reported, including discrimination against Muslims or incidents at mosques,” the spokesman said.

“[The hotline] can help people who experience discrimination to give their account, but we encourage these people to come to us as well. We can only take action, get a picture of problems in society and respond to them if we know what is going on.”

Xavi recalls Veerman, keeps faith with Van Dijk in Oranje squad

September 18, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

New Netherlands head coach Xavi Hernández has recalled Joey Veerman to the squad for the opening Nations League match against Germany next week.

The Borussia Dortmund midfielder, who has won 17 international caps, was left out of the squad for this summer’s World Cup in North America after falling out with Xavi’s predecessor Ronald Koeman.

The Spanish coach’s first squad is a mixture of youth and experience, with some senior players retained while others have made way for the Eredivisie’s young stars. Three members of the 26-man squad play their football in the Netherlands, while half are with clubs in the English Premier League.

Captain Virgil van Dijk is expected to win his 97th cap in Amsterdam next Thursday, ending speculation that the 35-year-old was considering retiring from international football.

Tijjani Reijnders and Crysencio Summerville have also kept their places despite moving to Saudi Arabia in the summer, in a departure from Koeman’s policy of not picking players from the Saudi league.

But there is no place for the Netherlands’ all-time leading scorer, Memphis Depay, who has struggled with injuries this year.

Twente’s veteran striker Wout Weghorst has also been left out, while Feyenoord’s in-form striker Gjivai Zechiël and PSV winger Ruben van Bommel, son of World Cup finalist Mark, are also in line to win their first caps.

After playing Germany in the Amsterdam Arena, Oranje will travel to Belgrade to take on Serbia on Sunday in their second match.

Full squad:

Goalkeepers: Mark Flekken (Bayer Leverkusen), Robin Roefs (Sunderland), Bart Verbruggen (Brighton & Hove Albion)

Defenders: Nathan Ake (Fenerbahçe), Virgil van Dijk (Liverpool), Denzel Dumfries (Real Madrid), Jeremie Frimpong (Liverpool), Lutsharel Geertruida (PSV), Jorrel Hato (Chelsea), Jan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham Hotspur), Jurrien Timber (Arsenal), Micky van de Ven (Tottenham Hotspur)

Midfielders: Ryan Gravenberch (Liverpool), Teun Koopmeiners (Juventus), Tijjani Reijnders (Al-Qadsiah), Kenneth Taylor (Lazio), Quinten Timber (Crystal Palace), Joey Veerman (Borussia Dortmund), Gjivai Zechiel (Feyenoord)

Forwards: Justin Kluivert (Bournemouth), Ruben van Bommel (PSV), Brian Brobbey (Sunderland), Cody Gakpo (Liverpool), Noa Lang (Napoli), Donyell Malen (AS Roma), Crysencio Summerville (Al-Hilal)

item.title: Dutch housing update: money for new homes, rising interest rates
item.description:
Partner content

Dutch housing update: money for new homes, rising interest rates

September 18, 2026

There was some good news for home buyers in this week’s budget with the announcement of a massive financial package to boost new residential development. There are also signs that house price rises are slowing down, although interest rates are shooting up and the issue of foundations continues to be confusing. This and more in the latest housing news round-up.

Budget briefing

There was not much in the way of direct measures impacting on the Dutch housing market in this week’s budget. For example, the government did not announce any new changes to the current mortgage interest deduction set up, although there will be a slight rise in income tax rate in the first and second tax bands, which will have a minimal impact on your rebate.

Housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan did come up with a string of measures she hopes will boost supply in the rental sector and new construction, and is pressing ahead with plans to cut the property transfer tax for holiday homes and investment properties from 8% to 7%.

Most relevant for would-be home buyers? “Plenty of investment in large scale developments of new homes, so if you are looking for a new-build property, you could be lucky – although the changes will take time to filter through,” says Matthijs van der Heijden, a mortgage advisor with Expat Mortgages, which has been helping internationals buy a home for over 20 years.

The government is also putting a further €100 million into a special fund to help first-time buyers get a foot on the housing ladder.

Interest rate increases

Over the past 18 months interest rates have been pretty stable but have been trending upwards since the second quarter of the year, and are currently rising sharply as geopolitical uncertainties continue.

“We are not yet seeing these higher rates have an impact on house prices,” says Matthijs, “but there does seem to be a little bit of room for negotiation. And some buyers are able to have a second viewing of a property before they decide whether to put in a bid.

“So there is more opportunity for people who don’t want to rush into a purchase. And we have noticed that some estate agents are helping their clients to negotiate on or just under the asking price.”

The higher interest rates are also making it more important to have some savings if you are planning to buy, just to keep your costs as low as you can. “If you have €50,000 that you can put down towards the cost of your house, that means €50,000 you won’t have to borrow at well over 4% interest,” Matthijs points out.

Ask your mortgage-related questions

Expat Mortgages will be at the IamExpat Fair in Eindhoven on October 3, so come along and meet the team in person, or sign up for an online or in person webinar, such as the one on September 30. “Getting out and meeting people is a terrific experience,” says Matthijs. “The first thing we tell prospective home buyers is that they should realise it will be a very different experience than in their home countries.”

Seminars, whether online or in person, are a great way of getting direct answers to your questions and sharing your experiences with others. “We also try to focus on the more specific situations – people who have not even moved here yet, and entrepreneurs who may not have been active in the Netherlands for more than a year, when most banks want three years,” says Matthijs.

“We’ve also seen an increase in the number of PhD students wanting to buy, and banks are becoming a little bit more lenient. They used to say ‘no permanent contract, no mortgage,’ but that is changing as well.”

More homes on the market?

Despite there being room for negotiation in some parts of the market, the shortage of cheaper homes to buy is continuing, and single people or single-income families wanting to buy a home are still facing an uphill struggle. Demand continues to be very high for properties at the lower end of the market.

“Things have been very slow over the summer, but now more people are getting out there and looking,” says Matthijs. “And you can still expect to have to overbid if you are looking at cheaper properties. Much depends on what areas you are looking in as well.”

The fundamentals of foundations

Since April, banks have been taking more account of a property’s foundations when deciding whether or not to back a mortgage application. As yet, says Matthijs, there is no overall consensus about what to do if a property’s foundations are in need of urgent, or not-so-urgent, action. “It is primarily the bigger banks which have been the frontrunners on this,” says Matthijs. “It is very early days.”

“However, you can assume if the report shows there is €100,000 worth of repairs which need to be done before the house is properly stable, the banks are going to wonder how this is going to be paid. This could be done, for example, by increasing your mortgage loan – although many people are nowadays stretched to capacity because of the high house prices – or through having the savings in your bank account. One way or another, your bank will want to know if you can pay for the work.”

Are you thinking about buying a home in the Netherlands? Make an appointment to talk directly to a mortgage advisor and find out how much you can borrow.

Weekend will be mix of sun and showers, temperatures around 18C

The Dutch meteorological institute is predicting a mix of showers and sunshine for the weekend.

There is still a chance of showers in the northeast of the country on Friday, according to KNMI but the evening will largely be dry. The afternoon temperature will remain around 18°C, with strong winds later in the evening.

On Saturday, there will be sun in the southeast but the rest of the country will see mostly cloudy skies. By the afternoon, there will be a chance of showers.

The north will see highs of 19°C while the southern part of the country will get up to 22°C.

Saturday evening will see rainstorms, including moderately strong winds along the coast.

Sunday bring more run but also more sunshine, with highs around 18°C.

item.title: Courts asked to shut 130 farms for breaching nitrogen limits
item.description:
Courts asked to shut 130 farms for breaching nitrogen limits

September 18, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Around 130 farmers risk being forced to give up their businesses after environmental group Mobilisation for the Environment (MOB) petitioned regional courts to tear up their nature permits, according to an investigation by RTL.

The organisation has started legal action in 10 provinces since 2023, asking judges to withdraw the permits of farms that exceed the limits for nitrogen depositions near Natura 2000 conservation areas.

Provincial governments have so far rejected applications from MOB, arguing that the cabinet in The Hague is working on a voluntary buyout scheme and other measures to reduce cattle numbers and nitrogen pollution.

Farmers must reduce ammonia emissions by 42% to 46% by 2035, compared to 2019 levels, under the latest package announced by agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen in June. The measures still have to be put before parliament.

The failure of successive cabinets to come up with a definitive plan since the Council of State ruled the system for issuing nature permits illegal in 2019 has prompted MOB to take the provinces to court.

Concentration in south

The majority of requests were made in the southern provinces of Noord-Brabant, Limburg, Gelderland and Overijssel, where pig, poultry and cattle farming is concentrated.

Noord-Brabant decided to withdraw its permits in July after a deadline of a year to settle the issue with MOB expired.

Van Essen said earlier this month that court orders to shut down farms were “exactly what we’re trying to prevent” with the government’s package of measures, which include a 5% to 10% across the board cut to livestock numbers as a last resort.

But Chris Backes, professor of environmental law at Utrecht University, questioned whether the plans went far enough.

“Measures by the national government are only part of the solution,” he told RTL. “For some nature areas they are sufficient, according to research by the Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency (PBL).

“But in most cases the provinces will have to implement additional measures.”
